utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today we are going to start another chapter in the history of this Tribunal. We are starting a new case, the Naser Oric case. So, Mr. Registrar, could I ask you to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And I welcome you all. Before we proceed any further, I want to make sure that the accused can follow the proceedings in his own language. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the interpreters are receiving ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can follow the proceedings in a language I speak, and I can understand everything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at any time in the course of the proceedings today and on every day that the Tribunal -- the Trial Chamber will be sitting, you encounter problems, difficulties, in receiving interpretation in your own language, please draw our attention immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There will be no problems, but I will draw your attention should there be any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: For the Prosecution: My name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney, together with Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, Ms. Patricia Sellers, attorneys; and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, she is our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, my learned friends. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with my colleague John Jones, an attorney-at-law from Great Britain, I am defending Naser Oric. The members of my team are Geoffrey Roberts, our case manager, and Ms. Jasmina Cosic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, madam, and thank you. Good morning to the rest of the team too, and welcome. Before we proceed any further, those of you who were present during the pre-trial conference know exactly who we are, but I suppose I should proceed with a very, very short, brief introduction of myself and the other two Judges that together with me compose this Trial Chamber. My name is Carmel Agius and I come from the island of Malta, where I was -- I sat as the -- practically the Deputy Chief Justice on the Court of Appeal and also on the Constitutional Court, the Court of Appeal, and basically all its jurisdictions, including criminal jurisdictions. I have been a Judge of this Tribunal since November of 2001. My right, I present to you Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt from Denmark. Judge Brydensholt was elected as an ad litem Judge in this Tribunal way back in 2001, like I was. And before coming to this Tribunal, he served as a Judge but also as chairman of several important commissions, including the Danish Institute of Holocaust and Genocide Studies, he's a member of the Penal Reform International, and at some point in time he was also part of the Danish government assistance project to developing countries working as an advisor on the reorganisation of the judicial system of several countries, particularly Uganda and Mozambique. Judge Albin Eser, to my left, is an old friend of mine. He comes from Germany. Judge Eser too was elected as an ad litem Judge in 2001. Apart from being a Judge, he has also been the president of one of the most prestigious institutions in Germany, and that's the Max Planck Institute. He's an expert on international criminal law. I must say I am lucky the second time to be flanked with two very, very, very good Judges. Having said that, I think we will proceed with our agenda for today. Today's sitting will be divided basically into two parts, or three parts. The next part will be precisely our -- there are some matters that we've discussed amongst ourselves and we decided to raise today, hoping that by raising them today we should be in a position to come to a conclusion -- to conclude them tomorrow. And they need to be concluded as early as possible. And then we will immediately move to the opening statement of the Prosecutor, to be followed by the opening statement of the Defence. I take it, but I just want to confirm it, that your client will not be availing himself of the option and the right that he has to address the Trial Chamber. And this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Let's start with the housekeeping matters, some of which we will deal with today, others obviously will be dealt with tomorrow. There is, as you know, a motion -- a confidential motion, Prosecution motion, for leave to amend their list of witnesses, which was filed on the 28th of September. We have gone also through your response, which was filed on the 1st of October. I want first to make sure if there are any -- if there's any updating on this list, which I understand there is, that you would like to put us in the picture in for today, Mr. Wubben, because I understand that the list you have provided has somewhat changed or that you were supposed to liaise with the Defence by a certain date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you mean the sequence order of the witnesses, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's one of it. But also you asked in your motion for authorisation to add to the number of witnesses that you had on your list. And I want to make sure whether you have given the Defence all the information that they required of you, which was supposed to be given -- to be handed by a certain date, and I don't know if it has been handed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we received the response by the Defence, and the response showed us that they questioned the fact that we disclosed the statements that belonged to those witnesses. We checked it out and it was true, we didn't disclose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you done so now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We have done so in the meanwhile, several days ago, but I received some kind of information that yesterday or the day before they received it. It has to be confirmed. But anyhow we did our best and we apologise to the Bench and to Defence that we took it that we disclosed it but we didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones, I don't know who is going to respond to this. First I want to make sure that you have actually received the statements of the witnesses that you had made reservations on. And what is -- whether you maintain the position or whether you want to revise your position so that tomorrow we will be in a position to decide this issue, this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Well, if I might start with Racine Manas, which is perhaps easiest. Your Honours referred to the Prosecution motion of last Tuesday, the 28th of September. And you'll see in that motion, on footnote 5, page 4, it was very clearly stated that the declaration of Racine Manas would be provided to the Defence by the 1st of October, 2004. It was clear and categorical. The 1st of October came and went, we waited, and we considered that if we received the statement on that day, although it was only a week, which wasn't a lot of time to prepare for the first witness, that we would be able to handle it. But because of the history of not receiving statements on time, we protected our position by filing the response which we filed. On Monday, the 4th of October, we received a draft declaration and a draft spreadsheet, 48 pages, with hundreds of items accompanying the statement of Ms. Manas. Of course, until we receive the final statement and spreadsheet, we can't prepare for cross-examination, because some things might change, a lot of things might change, everything might change. So we have been waiting for the final draft -- sorry, the final statement, which you received yesterday, I believe. We found it in our locker this morning, and that's for the first witness in this trial which opens today. We've looked at it, we've considered it, and we consider we will be in a position to cross-examine Ms. Manas on Friday. But we considered that it's nothing short of scandalous that we received the statement for the first witness so late in the day. We're in your hands, but as I say, we are now willing to proceed with that witness. As far as the other statements are concerned, the position is the same, that the Prosecution's motion stated that the witness's statements have been disclosed to us. As you've heard from Mr. Wubben just now, they haven't been. We received, I believe it was yesterday, the English versions of statements of -- I'm not sure if I need to read the names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can skip the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We haven't received the Bosnian language versions. But again we've considered the position and we are -- we don't object to any of the witnesses. We can go ahead with them. I mention all this to a certain extent by way of background because Your Honours will have seen, or your senior legal officer will have seen letters copied between the parties in which the Prosecution emphatically state that we've received -- that they are disclosing a second time material to us which we have said we have not received before. I would just make the point that given this history of the Prosecution failing to meet its own deadlines, admittedly not disclosing statements which they claim to disclose, they should be a little more circumspect about saying that we've received things when we haven't. Our house is in order; they should put theirs in order. Having said that, that is our position and we are prepared to go ahead. I also mention that by way of background because we've received a revised witness list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm coming to that because I have my own questions on that. Let's conclude this first part. In other words, do I take it that there is now at this very moment no objection to the Prosecution's motion to amend the Prosecution list of witnesses, to wit, by the addition of the witnesses that are mentioned in the motion? In other words, we can proceed with our decision which can be handed orally tomorrow after -- during the housekeeping section of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Indeed you have seen that for two of the witnesses we are happy even with their declarations going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am coming to those as well. That's Kelly and Tedder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I also wanted to know, once you've brought this matter up, whether we are to take this as meaning that you are not going to cross-examination these two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's right. But I should say that for the other witnesses, we do, of course, hope to receive the Bosnian language versions as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, Mr. Jones. But I just wanted to make sure that you do not want to cross-examine Messrs. Kelly and Tedder. So Mr. Wubben and Madam Vidovic, we will decide this motion tomorrow during the sitting. We will not be handing down a written decision, we will restrict it to an oral one. That basically brings me to the second matter. We had a list of witnesses, the first batch of witnesses that the Prosecution intended to bring forward. There are two main issues I would like to address and then we will address the matter more thoroughly tomorrow, but we need to be briefed on these today. Number one is that in that list there is mention of two witnesses that the Prosecution is seeking to bring forward under Rule 92(C), 92 bis (C). We haven't authorised that the testimony of these witnesses be tendered under Rule 92 bis (C) as yet. So perhaps you should enlighten us on this issue first and foremost because we still have to debate whether the testimony of these two persons can be presented in this case under the conditions that you are pretending, Mr. Wubben. That's number one. Second thing is that I was informed a few minutes before we started the sitting -- when I say "I," we were informed, Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser as well. We were having a meeting with our staff early this morning and we were told that the list that you had handed and which was made available up to yesterday was going to -- has been revised and that today we will be receiving a fresh list. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is the -- the substance of the change?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The substance of the change will be that from the 14th of October we start with Mr. Dragan Djuric, Simic subsequently, Milenja Mitrovic, and Rankovic, that's from another crime base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just make sure none of these witnesses enjoy protective measures by the way of pseudonyms in particular. That's why I have been avoiding mentioning names. So make sure that when you mention names, none of them are protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When Your Honour asked me for the changes, it means for me that we will turn over to another crime base and relate it to another attack than first envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has the Defence been provided with a copy of the revised list of first number of witnesses that you intend to bring forward or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. According to me, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We received it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't received it as yet, so we need to have it in front of us before we can proceed with the debate. Is that the list or the statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will start with your investigator, Ms. Manas, on Friday. This is definitely not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is, I take it, the investigator that we asked for?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Going through the list of documents and confirming to us provenance and chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I think -- yes, is there anything you would like to add, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just two points. The first concerns the expert witness, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We made it very plain to the Prosecution that we would require two days to cross-examine him. That might sound exceptional given the length of the examination-in-chief, but firstly we have agreed and we are happy for Dr. Gow to be led through a large part of his evidence in chief precisely to save the court's time because we will need a lot of time with him. It's a matter, I can go into it at another time, perhaps, but we have been clear; we require two days and this schedule doesn't allow for that; it would allow us only to cross-examine him for the rest of the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come to that later, Mr. Jones. However, once you mention Mr. Gow, may I draw your attention, Mr. Wubben, Mr. Jones, that it seems that Mr. Gow deals to a large extent in his expert report on the aspect of the internationality of the conflict, which is no longer on our table.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We beg to differ. Perhaps it was originally drafted with that context in mind, but essentially it's dealing with the whole historical, military, political background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a lot on the internationality of the conflict, particularly in regard to the involvement of the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We say that certainly doesn't drop out of the case as irrelevant because it is a very large part of the military context. It is something which, as will become apparent during our cross-examination, is very important, certainly to our case. We wouldn't agree that since there's no longer an international armed conflict being alleged that therefore his testimony assumes any less relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's a second point perhaps I should make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is the list we received before had the witnesses for Ratkovici first, followed by the Jezestica witnesses. We have, of course, been preparing for the last few days on the basis that the first witnesses would be testifying about Ratkovici. So of course, it creates additional difficulties for us to adapt, but of course we are in your hands, we will adapt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, Mr. Jones, there is enough time within which you can adapt, actually, because we have got the entire of next week dealing with witnesses that have got nothing to do with events such -- or crime based evidence. So I think that week can be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Unless I'm wrong, I think the first fact witness will be testifying on Thursday, according to this plan. Next Thursday. According to this plan. We would say he should be listed for the 15th so that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness number 6. Are you talking about witness number 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Between now and then you have more than a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course we're in trial and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but you have more than a week. And basically that witness and the -- we should dispose of by -- either on that same -- no, we can dispose of that witness by Friday, and that leaves you again more time for witness number 7 who then starts on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, and we do say that witness should be listed for the 15th of October so we have the 14th of October for Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So basically this -- yes, Mr. Wubben, I recognise you standing. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are just a couple of other matters. The first one refers to the Prosecution confidential motion for leave to add exhibits to its exhibit list. This, as you remember, we brought this up during the pre-trial conference. During the pre-trial conference the approach taken was that we should strive to have this determined before we start the trial. And I also gave you the opportunity to file a reply referenced to the objection raised by the Defence in relation to five of the proposed additional exhibits. To my knowledge, and I stand to be corrected, but to my knowledge until yesterday evening at least, I was not aware of any reply on your part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm mentioning this not because it would deprive me of any sleep but because, if this is the case, the deadline which you have in terms of Rule 126 (B) bis would have lapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did indeed return to this matter. Ms. Patricia Sellers will address this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The Prosecution is well aware of its obligation and yesterday we filed with the Registry motions that answered the questions that the Judges raised and also that the Defence raised in terms of the exhibit list. I believe that those responses are available to the Defence and to Your Honours as of today as soon as Registry as properly stamped them. In addition to that, Your Honour, I would like to say that we have also filed the response that Your Honours directed us pertaining to the pre-trial brief. There were some issues that you asked that we address. Yes, that was also filed, Your Honour, and should be available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Have you been served with these responses, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm just looking now at the Prosecution's reply to our response on the motion for leave to add exhibits. So I've just glanced at that. I don't know if it's something which Your Honour would like me to deal with now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, the only thing we were addressing this morning was to establish whether a response had been filed, in which case obviously we will address the matter tomorrow and, if possible, we will even reach a decision tomorrow on these matters. But be prepared to debate this particular issue tomorrow, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. And we have also received the motion regarding the pre-trial brief. So we have those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The last two things are the following: There is a Prosecution confidential motion for witness protection -- for witness protection. This was filed on the 28th of September. I'm just mentioning this motion. If there is no objection for the protective measures being sought, then you are invited to say so. It would spare you having to file a written response and it would spare us having to having to hand down a written decision. We will just decide it orally tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we strenuously object to one of the witnesses, protective measures for one of the witnesses, and we will be filing response by Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's do it this way: Tomorrow morning when we reconvene and start with the house -- finalising the housekeeping matters that are still pending, you will indicate to us the witness that you have -- you need to make submissions upon so that we can decide orally on the protective measures for the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Last matter on my agenda before we move to the next part is the Rule 92 bis (C) testimony. This is a very serious matter that we cannot possibly dispose of orally. It does require a thorough examination. I would like you to think on whether you require a special sitting to address this matter or whether you prefer to address it by means of written submissions. We are happy with either of the two, but we will need to decide this issue as early as possible since even the updated list of witnesses still indicate two of those witnesses as of being amongst the very first batch of witnesses to give evidence before this Tribunal. So we need to decide whether the request of the Prosecution can be met or whether it has to be turned down, in which case the Prosecution will reconsider the other options that they may have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, may I address that issue? We would like to inform the Defence at this point in time, too, that we are formulating a written response. There is more information that we would certainly like to impart to Your Honours concerning the witnesses. I believe there is an objection to the witness who is deceased where there is absolutely no question. We are more than willing to respond to that, and we have other information, other positions we would like to put forward to Your Honours. We would ask at this time period that possibly after receiving our written response, that we might discuss this matter in a different session, that it might be a bit too premature in this instance to go into some details that we would rather reserve after you've looked at our written response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, I take it that you are initiating the process --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between because you are overlapping and very fast --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... available to Your Honours by tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Ms. Sellers, and my apologies to the interpreters. Again, since this is mostly an English-speaking Chamber we do have the tendency not to allow a pause between one intervention and the other and that makes the lives of the interpreters difficult. So my apologies to them and let's try and avoid this happening again. So that basically deals with all the matters that we needed to raise. Now, we have - Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser and myself - discussed the procedure that is to be followed here, and we advised you that tomorrow we will be handing down orally a set of guidelines that relate to admissibility of evidence, evidence and procedure in general, and also the conduct that is expected from each one of us and of course of this trial. However, we discussed also the peculiarity of these proceedings which have their origin in the confirmation of the indictment which is then followed by the initial appearance of the accused. And it is on that occasion that the indictment is read out, if at all, because sometimes the accused waives his right to have the indictment read. In all other domestic jurisdictions, basically what you have is that the beginning of the trial itself is marked by either the reading of the indictment, which in our case we are not going to do -- at least, we have decided that the public particularly should be made aware of what the accused is -- stands charged with, because as it is we are going to start a trial and I very much doubt how many of the people present in the gallery here, how many following the proceedings on transmissions in Yugoslavia and elsewhere can understand unless they really go into the records of this Tribunal and find out what the case is about. So what we agreed was that today, before I give the floor to the Prosecution to present the case, make their opening speech, I will -- on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and of myself, I will briefly give you a summary of what this case is all about and what Mr. Naser Oric is being charged with. It will not be a long presentation, but I think it will help the audience understand better what are the significant features of this case. The accused, Naser Oric, is of course aware of the indictment, also of the amendments made to the indictment, and he has pleaded not guilty to all the counts that have been brought against him by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. The accused is a Bosnian Muslim. He was born on the 3rd of March, 1967, in Potocari, and Potocari is in the Srebrenica municipality, now part of Republika Srpska. During the period relevant to the indictment, that is the 10th of June of 1992 to the 20th of March of 1993, the accused is alleged to have held various positions of authority within the local police and the local military units. On the 8th of April, 1992, he was appointed chief of the Potocari police substation, and on the 17th of April, 1992, he became commander of the Potocari Territorial Defence unit. On the 20th of May, 1992, he was appointed commander of the Srebrenica Territorial Defence headquarters, which was renamed headquarters of the Srebrenica Armed Forces on the 3rd of September of 1992. On the 1st of July, 1992, he became a member of the War Presidency in Srebrenica. This is a kind of a Crisis Staff. In early November 1992 he became commander of the joint armed forces of Srebrenica subregion. And finally, on the 12th of July, 1994, even though this goes beyond the period of our indictment, the accused was promoted to the rank of brigadier general. The indictment that governs this trial relates to incidents which the Prosecution alleges to have taken place between, as I said, the 10th of June, 1992, and the 20th of March, 1993, in the municipalities of Bratunac and Srebrenica. These municipalities are all located in Eastern Bosnia, in Herzegovina, and basically they border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The accused is charged with six counts of violations of the laws and customs of war pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute. I'm going to divide these charges into two main series of incidents to which they relate. The first category of charges relate to murder and cruel treatment. The Prosecution alleges that between the 24th of September, 1992, and the 20th of March, 1993, members of the military police that were under the command and control of the accused detained several Bosnian Serb individuals in the Srebrenica police station and also in the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building. It is alleged by the Prosecution that these members of -- these Bosnian Serb individuals were subjected to physical abuse, serious suffering, serious injury to body and health, and inhumane treatment. In addition, the Prosecution alleges that, while in detention, 11 Bosnian Serb individuals were subjected to such mistreatment. I'm going to mention the names of these individuals: Nedeljko Radic, Slavoljub Zikic, Zoran Brankovic, Nevenko Bubanj, Veselin Sarac, Ilija Ivanovic, Ratko Nikolic, Rado Pejic, Stanko Mitrovic, Miloje Obradovic, Mile Trifunovic. In addition, the Prosecution alleges that seven Bosnian Serb men were killed. The names of these seven men are the following: Dragotin Kukic, Jakov Djokic, Dragan Ilic, Milisav Milovanovic, Kostadin Popovic, Branko Sekulic, and finally, Bogdan Zivanovic. The accused is essentially charged with murder in count 1, murder being a violation of the laws or customs of war pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute of this Tribunal. The accused is also charged in relation to these events in count 2 with cruel treatment, cruel treatment being a violation of the laws or customs of war pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute. That's the first category of events to which two of the counts relate. The other category can be practically described as wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages, or devastation not justified by military necessity and plunder of public or private property. Essentially, the Prosecution alleges that between the 10th of June, 1992, and February 1993 Bosnian Muslim armed units under the command and control of the accused engaged in various military operations against the Bosnian Serb army - in the course of the proceedings we will be referring to this army as the VRS - and that in the course of such actions, they burned or otherwise destroyed and plundered 13 predominantly Bosnian Serb villages and/or hamlets in the municipalities of Srebrenica and Bratunac. I'm going to mention these villages or hamlets: Ratkovici, Bradevina, Ducici, Gornji Ratkovici, Jezestica, Osmace, Fakovici, Radijevici, Divovici, Bjelovac, Sikirici, Kravica and Siljkovici. In relation to these events, in count 3 and 5 of the indictment the accused is being charged with wanton destruction of cities, towns or villages, not justified by military necessity, this being a violation of the laws or customs of war pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute. Always in relation to these events in counts 4 and 6 of the indictment, the accused is being charged with plunder of public or private property, this also being a violation of the laws or customs of war pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute. The accused is being charged under two modes of liability. In the first place, he's being charged criminally responsible by virtue of his superior command. We refer to this as superior responsibility or command responsibility. And this mode of responsibility is being charged or alleged by the Prosecution by virtue of Article 7(3) of our Statute. Basically I will explain what this means. The accused is primarily charged with the crimes alleged in the indictment pursuant to this mode of liability. Basically this means that the Prosecution alleges that the accused, by virtue of his position and authority as commander, had de facto and de jure command over all units that were operating in his area of command and responsibility and that he exercised effective control over his subordinates. The Prosecution therefore alleges that the accused is criminally responsible as a superior for the acts of his subordinates, both at the Srebrenica police station and in the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building. Basically this applies to the crimes of murder and cruel treatment that is counts 1 and counts 2 that I mentioned to you earlier. The Prosecution is also alleging superior command responsibility in relation to the military operations in the 13 predominantly Bosnian Serb villages and hamlets that I mentioned earlier on. And therefore, superior command is also being invoked in relation to counts 3 and counts 4. Overall the Prosecution is also charging the accused with individual criminal responsibility. This is something different. And this kind of criminal responsibility is contemplated and regulated by Article 7(1) of our Statute. I will very briefly explain what this means. Basically, the Prosecution is alleging that the accused is individually criminally responsible pursuant to the Article or sub-Article that I have just mentioned, namely for having instigated and aided and abetted through his acts of commission or through his acts of omission the crimes of wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages not justified by military necessity - that's in count 5 - and plunder of property in the course of military operations in the villages of Fakovici on the 5th of October, 1992; Bjelovac, between the 14th and 19th of December, 1992; and Kravica and Jezestica on the 7th and 8th of January, 1992 [sic]. These events are contemplated in count 6 of the indictment. And that explains to the public the substance of the case which we will be hearing. Tomorrow, as I explained earlier, the first part of the sitting will be dedicated to guidelines and then we will organise the rest of the trial and you will also have an indication of how long the Prosecution case is expected to last. And this will be a time limit which you are -- you will be asked to stick to as much as possible. So having said so, I now invite the -- Mr. Wubben to open -- make his opening statement on behalf of the Prosecution. We have until the rest of the morning, of the sitting, to finish. I take it that you require about 90 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a case about a young commander who became a warlord. In accepting his role as commander, he amassed authority and power. War crimes of murder, wanton destruction, and plunder were committed under his command. The Prosecution opens its case today against the accused Naser Oric, former bodyguard, former police officer, former brigadier general from the Srebrenica municipality of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The facts of this case originate in the municipality and surrounding areas of Srebrenica located in the far Eastern Bosnia that borders on Serbia. In 1992, the former Yugoslavia witnessed the crushing clash of three groups separated by their political vision, ethnic identification, and religious practices. Armed conflict engulfed the entire country. Atrocious crimes were committed by and against Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Croats as the country spiraled out of control and descended into inter-ethnic fighting, as shown on the map that you will see. The nations of Serbia and Croatia backed their proxy sides of the struggle and entangled themselves into the inter-ethnic destruction of the Yugoslav peoples. Lives were lost, families destroyed, livelihoods ruined. Ethnic cleansing, the removal of inhabitants from their territories, brutalised and spared no group. The territorial divisions followed the ethnic divide, also shown on the map. Places such as Foca, Brcko, Mostar, Vukovar, and Srebrenica resound with the horrors of ethnic division and atrocities. The Tribunal was created by the Security Council to redress the breach of peace on behalf of the international community as a whole. The international community encompassed the citizens of the former Yugoslavia. A judicial mandate was provided to examine the allegations of war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed during the armed conflict. The Tribunal was mandated to judge individuals accused of international crimes recalling the maxim that crimes, international crimes, are committed by individuals. Neither nations nor ethnic groups are collectively accused nor collectively condemned for such crimes. In March 1992, the Yugoslav army, the JNA, together with the Serb Territorial Defence of the Republic of Srpska army, captured and occupied the town of Srebrenica. The determined offensive power of the territorial offence units of the Srebrenica municipality forced the retreat of the JNA and Bosnian Serb forces out of the Srebrenica town. Starting in May 1992 the accused, Naser Oric, became the instrumental soldier in forcing the retreat of the Bosnian Serb army and leading the attacks by the Bosnian army. By January 1993, the Srebrenica pocket, or enclave, was bare of Bosnian Serbs and exists thus. In the winter of 1993 the Bosnian Serb army began to regroup after a series of defeats by soldiers under the military command of Oric. By April 1993, UNPROFOR undertook the demilitarisation of the Srebrenica zone. Your Honours, by 1992 three facts were not in dispute: First, from 1992 and until 1995 Naser Oric repeatedly accepted and assumed increased and widening military command of soldiers. Second, Naser Oric crucially, as a commander, was bound by laws of war, both by customary international law and by Bosnian decrees that incorporated those customary principles into the national governing law. Third, Naser Oric crucially, as a soldier and a commander, was duty-bound to follow Bosnian army military orders that specifically directed him to obey international law. Naser Oric, a former JNA corporal, a personal security guard, and then a police officer, voluntarily and knowingly accepted and assumed wartime command and responsibility for soldiers in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Prosecution's case against Naser Oric focuses on his acts and his failure to act when he commanded the Srebrenica Municipal Territorial Defence, the Srebrenica armed forces, the Srebrenica subregion, the 8th Operational Group, and later, the 28th Division of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Prosecution will show that: As a commander, Oric did not obey or enforce the laws of war when his troops attacked Serb villages in the Srebrenica area; he did not enforce the laws when his soldiers destroyed, burned, and looted villages. Naser Oric selectively applied the Geneva Conventions. The accused invoked the law to detain children and females, yet he ignored the Geneva Conventions and allowed his soldiers to brutalise Serbian male prisoners. The accused failed, in general, to prevent and rein in the lawlessness of his soldiers and failed specifically to punish his soldiers who committed crimes against Bosnian Serbs. The Prosecution's evidence will clarify why the accused allowed his soldiers to proceed with impunity. The criminality suited him and furthered the accused's war policy and aims. Oric's aim was to clear the Bosnian Serb dwellers from the Srebrenica territory, to ensure that Serb villagers and peasants would not return to their homes. His soldiers plundered Bosnian Serb property and destroyed dwellings and usually burned what was left standing. Oric's soldiers repeatedly carried out a three-step plan: Step one, soldiers attacked the village; step two, after the fighting ceased, soldiers and civilians plundered the village; step three, soldiers and civilians destroyed the village, usually by burning. In the midst of the three-step process, many villagers were killed. The Trial Chamber will notice a pattern of fighting for food and fighting with fire. Oric employed another policy for wartime prisoners. Male and female Bosnian Serbs were kept in Srebrenica detention facilities. Naser Oric's guards, police officers subordinated to him, brutalised and terrorised the male detainees, leading to the death of seven prisoners. The accused knew about and tolerated the beatings, the brutalisation and the deaths of the male prisoners. Oric only kept the Serb male and female prisoners to trade for Muslim prisoners or dead Muslim soldiers. Clearing the Serbs from Srebrenica municipality relieved Oric of having to consider, as occupying commanders do, the needs of a large-scale detention for occupied Bosnian Serb villagers. The relatively moderate number of Bosnian Serb prisoners gave Naser Oric the manoeuvrability to broker prisoner exchanges with the Bosnian Serb army. Hence, the accused had no reason in his plan to punish his subordinates for the beatings and killings of the Serbian male detainees as long as he kept some male prisoners alive for exchange. Oric failed to obey or to enforce the laws and customs of war, whether commanding on the battlefield or being in command of the detention facilities. Laws presented more of an irritant than an obligation for Oric. The office of the Prosecutor wishes to stress that the laws of armed conflict are customary and in their most basic application are binding upon all soldiers during wartime. The laws exist to be enforced now at this very minute while I address Your Honours. All soldiers and all commanders who, while we speak, are engaged in armed conflict, are duty-bound to respect, obey, follow, and enforce these principles. Starting in 1992 and throughout the winter and spring of 1993, Eastern Bosnia, including the municipalities of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Vlasenica were swallowed up in heightened armed conflict. Thousands of Bosnian Muslim refugees swarmed into the town of Srebrenica. Thousands of Bosnian Serbs fled the town of Srebrenica. War was accompanied by chaotic and unstable circumstances. Severe humanitarian conditions prevailed. Death, hunger, disease, displacement, and fear, anger, and immense sorrow abounded. The Prosecution underscores the gravity of the war-related circumstances in Srebrenica to Your Honours on the Trial Chamber to stress an essential principle. The laws of armed conflict are specifically designed to come into force and be applied during wartime, during those moments when societies devolve into killings and destruction and mayhem. In particular, brigadier and wartime commanders are specifically charged with ensuring that war is regulated by the very laws of armed conflict that concern this Trial Chamber. Naser Oric understood this wartime obligation but consistently opted time and time again to ignore and thus breach his responsibility as a commanding officer. Your Honours must question the circular logic of the accused. Is it because he was fighting a war that Naser Oric was too busy to apply the laws of war? The accused knowingly violated, distorted, and ignored the law because it served his purposes. Disregarding the law of war bode well for the mode and manner that he wanted to wage battle and how he ordered his men to fight the war. Absent the weight of law, Oric became lawless. From June 1992 until March 1993, Oric met with lawless success. He routed the Bosnian Serb army and he cleared Srebrenica of its Bosnian Serb inhabitants. By March 1993, Oric exchanged all Bosnian Serb prisoners, those who were still alive, from the Srebrenica detention centre. Disobeying the laws of armed conflict offered Naser Oric an advantage. Engaging in optional obedience to the law increased Oric's military and political power. Naser Oric became the man with uncontested command in Srebrenica and undisputed control of Srebrenica. Did Naser Oric know that his conduct violated international law? The Prosecution's evidence will show that he did. Did he know that his soldiers destroyed and burned the Bosnian Serb villages? The Prosecution's evidence will show that he did. Naser Oric ordered soldiers not to burn the village until they were plundered. On one occasion, Naser Oric ordered the soldiers not to burn the village on the first day because his soldiers needed to spend the night in the houses. Then the houses and barns could be torched. Did he know about the burning? The Prosecution's evidence will show that Oric told General Sefer Halilovic in June of 1993 that the Bosnian Serb army would "burn like we did in January of 1993." Did he know about the plunder? The Prosecution's evidence will show that he told Muslim soldiers that they would attack for the food, in particular on Orthodox Christmas. Naser Oric was advised by Muslim officers to stop the burning, the looting, the pillaging. He listened but did do nothing. Did Naser Oric know that the prison guards beat and terrorised the detainees? The Prosecution's evidence will show that Naser Oric saw the brutalised prisoners and chose not to stop the beatings. He knew the violate behaviour of his soldiers, such as the brutal soldier named Kemo. Did he know about the cruel treatment and the deaths in the prisons? Oric spoke with the detainees about the dead prisoners who could no longer be used for exchange. An angered Naser Oric, surrendered by his prison guards, even kicked and struck detainees. Fellow Muslim fighters implored Naser Oric to utilise experienced army officers to maintain discipline and compensate for his inexperience. Fellow Muslim fighters resigned from the Srebrenica armed forces headquarters' staff to protest of the commanders ignoring the lawlessness of Muslim soldiers in Srebrenica. Naser Oric rejected the advice to maintain discipline and compensate for his inexperience. Naser Oric knew of the chaos because he inflamed it and it led to resignations at the headquarters staff. Fellow Muslim fighters advised Naser Oric to set up military courts in Srebrenica to address the widespread lawlessness. Naser Oric refused to do so. When he set up a military tribunal, it was not to judge the crimes against Bosnian Serbs but to remove the Muslim military enemies, his enemies. Of course Naser Oric knew about the crimes, but he knew -- he chose not to investigate nor punish his subordinates. He did not stop civilians from participating in crimes alongside of his soldiers. Rather, the Prosecution will show, that he promoted and facilitated and abetted civilian crimes. Naser Oric was not merely a commander. In the field and at headquarters, he held uncontested military authority in Srebrenica. Because of his membership on the War Presidency, he held uncontested political power. Naser Oric was the reigning authority, the reigning lord, a warlord. What is a warlord? The warlord is a supreme military leader exercising civil power and accountable to no one. The Prosecution would like to review the charges against the accused and express its position on a few but important points of international law that will guide Your Honours' evaluation of the evidence. It is self-evident that the Prosecution appreciates the burden upon her and that she is bound to prove in a case against Naser Oric the standard beyond a reasonable doubt. The Prosecution shall discharge this burden. The Prosecution has charged Naser Oric in count 1 with murder. Seven Bosnian Serb males died in Srebrenica detention facilities. Between September 1992 and March 1993, prisoners captured during the attacks were kept in two locations: First in the Srebrenica police building; later men, women, and children were held in cells in the building behind the Srebrenica municipal building. In September of 1992 a prisoner by the name of Dragutin Kukic was beaten to death in the Srebrenica police station by Kemo, a notoriously cruel guard. Naser Oric knew about Kemo and knew about Kukic's death. Another prisoner, Kostadin Popovic was imprisoned after the attack on Kravica in January 1993. Kostadin Popovic's body was exhumed. Dr. Stankovic performed an autopsy that concluded that Kostadin Popovic's head was split in two. His death was caused by cerebral damage, wounds that are consistent with beatings. Naser Oric knew about the deaths because there were prisoners who could not use these prisoners in exchange for captured Muslim soldiers. Other Serbian prisoners, namely Jakov Djokic, Dragan Ilic, Milisav Milanovic, Branko Sekulic, and Bogdan Zivanovic died in detention from daily brutally beating. Each man died because of the blows of the subordinates of Naser Oric. The male prisoners who did not die still did not escape unending cruelty. In count 2, the Prosecution charged the accused with cruel treatment for the beatings with iron bars and wooden poles, the forced extraction of teeth, and broken jaws. On numerous occasions the men were rendered unconscious. One prisoner remembers that "every one of us were bloody. Blood was everywhere; on the floor, on the walls. Blood came from everyone and was on our clothes." There were also female prisoners. Yes, it is in the Prosecution's evidence that Naser Oric imprisoned women and children in another cell down the hallway from where the males were held. One 12-year-old girl stated that, "I could hear the noises of the men being beaten in the other cell. I recognised my grandfather moaning in pain. Every night and every day the men were beaten. I could hear the noises and it was horrible." The evidence will demonstrate that Naser Oric knew about the murder of male prisoners and the cruel treatment inflicted by the guards upon those males that inexplicably survived the detention. At times the guards allowed civilians to come into the cells to assault the prisoners. Oric was often in the prison. He took pleasure in strolling down the hallway of the prison. He would tell detainees, male and female, who he was and the power that he had. Oric asked about the dead prisoners and knew about the beatings. The male detainees feared him because Naser Oric knew about the wild and violent behaviour of his guards like Kemo. He let Kemo stay. Oric could use his own eyes to see the faces of the male prisoners. He could look at them when he arranged their exchanges. Look at faces of two Serb prisoners a few days after their exchange; just use your eyes. In counts 3 and 5 the Prosecution accused Naser Oric of the wanton destruction of cities, towns, and villages that are not justified by military necessity. The predominantly Bosnian Serb towns of Rakovici, Jezestica, Fakovici, Bjelovac, and Kravica, and their surrounding hamlets were attacked by Muslim soldiers. The military objective of the fighting army of Bosnia and Herzegovina forces, ABiH, in Ratkovic was to gather weapons, gather food, expel the inhabitants, and move the Muslim front lines to the other side of the Bosnian Serb villages. Was there a military necessity to burn the villages? As emphasised earlier, the Muslim soldiers subordinate to Naser Oric burned the homes, barns, buildings, and sheds of these rural dwellers after the fighting ceased and the plunder was complete. Destruction was extensive. For example, in October 1992, as part of the attack on Fakovici and the neighbouring hamlets of Radijevici and Divovici, 80 per cent of the houses were destroyed by burning. In December 1992, half of the houses in Bjelovac and all of the houses in Sikirici were destroyed by fire. The evidence will prove that in January 1993 the whole village of Jezestica was burnt. The dwellings are not safe to shelter the Muslim refugee population. The cremated houses were to be home to no one and only served to dissuade their owners from returning home and living in the municipality. The Prosecution asserted earlier that Oric torched and destroyed the towns and hamlets to further his war plans, the three-step plan. The constant absence of distinguishing between military targets and civilian objects will prove that the destruction was unjustified by military necessity. Upon routing the opposing army, the Bosnian Serb troops, there lay no justification for the entire villages be destroyed. The armed presence of the village guards, consisting of a small number of elderly men left at home during the war, did not justify the torching of the hamlets. In counts 4 and 6 of the indictment the Prosecution accused Naser Oric of the plunder of public or private property. After the battle was over but before the fires were set, Bosnian Serb dwellings and buildings were systematically plundered. Muslim soldiers and civilians stripped the houses. Livestock and food were pillaged by soldiers as a final act of battle. Only pigs were destroyed and left. Goods were not temporarily requisitioned, they were outrightly plundered, permanently depriving their owners of ownership. Plunder was a wartime policy. Plunder and looting Serb villages further ensured that the Bosnian Serbs would not return home even to recover lifelong possessions. Plunder was a policy also because it served to feed the Bosnian Muslim refugees in Srebrenica. Plunder was a policy because it served to increase the supply of food for ABiH soldiers. Plunder was a policy even when humanitarian aid was delivered. Kravica was attacked for food on Orthodox Christmas. Plunder was not a war crime, according to Naser Oric, but a war policy. Are these ordinary crimes? Was the plunder only simple theft, simple property damage, and not serious crimes nor violations of the laws or customs of war? The Prosecution's position is that the ransacking, looting and pillaging of dwellings, houses, work places, barns, and sheds, the removal of furniture, stoves, family keepsakes, jewellery, money, and other possessions violated Article 3 of the Tribunal's Statute. The plunder of cattle and other farm animals, farm tools, and crops tractors, cars and wagons, constituted a net loss of material wealth for the victims and destroyed their ability to earn a livelihood in the future. The loss constituted a great value to the owners. The consequences of the loss for the owners were great. The laws of war protects property. Requisition of goods, a legitimate wartime deed, permits the use of public or private property but only when compensated by an occupying army. Requisition is the opposite of theft, plunder, and looting. Recognition of the distinction between crimes of plunder and permissible requisition are specifically designed to halt what Naser Oric unleashed rampaging for war booty. Respect for that distinction and obedience for such laws became too inconvenient for Naser Oric. Superior responsibility is found in Article 7(3) of the Statute. It informs that a superior, such as a commander, is liable for the crimes of his subordinates, if he knew or had reason to know that they were about to commit a crime under the Statute and failed to take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent the crimes or to punish the perpetrators thereof. Naser Oric was the superior, a commander of the Muslim troops in the Srebrenica municipality. He assumed command and amassed ever increasing, not decreasing, powers. The troops under his direct command numbered upwards of 10.000. Commencing on the 20th of May, 1992, he became the commander of the Srebrenica TO. Sefer Halilovic confirmed - did not appoint but confirmed - Oric's position as the commander of the Srebrenica TO on 27 June, 1992. On 1 July, 1992, Naser Oric became a member of the Srebrenica War Presidency in his capacity as commander. His de jure military command merged with his de facto powers that included growing political influence and control of civilian politics in Srebrenica. In November 1992, Oric was appointed commander of the subregion Srebrenica that covered areas in the surrounding municipalities of Bratunac, Vlasenica, and Zvornik. In January 1994, Oric was named commander of the 8th Operational Group of Srebrenica headquarters of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Oric remained in that position until he was appointed brigadier general on 12 July 1995. Until August 1995, Oric remained the commander of the renamed 8th Operational Group in what was then called the 28th Division of the ABiH. As commander, successively Oric had the obligation to ensure that his subordinates did not violate the laws of armed conflict. It was his obligation to prevent the commissions of crimes, and if those crimes occurred, he was to punish his subordinates for such crimes. This is in accordance with case law. A recent appellate decision re-affirmed these precepts of Article 7(3)'s superior responsibility. In addition to the superior/subordinate relationship, it holds that the responsibility of command are only enforceable if the commander knew or had reason to know that subordinates were about to commit crimes or that they had already committed these crimes. In the former case, Oric had a duty to prevent; in the latter case, he had a duty to punish. Our evidence will show that Naser Oric knew of the destruction of the towns and villages. Naser Oric arranged for the plundered goods to be taken and brought to Srebrenica. He or his soldiers divided up the plunder. Our evidence will show that he had actual knowledge for another reason. The burning and destroying lay beyond military necessity. While in certain places, the Muslim forces engaged with the Bosnian Serb army or the local town guard, the fighting that is mentioned in the indictment will show that the Muslims completely routed any armed opposition from the villages. When these villages were emptied of opposing fighters or local guards and absent of armed danger, the Muslim soldiers torched and destroyed houses. These acts did not win the battles; they were after and beyond the necessity of the battles. The Prosecution will show that the actual knowledge of Naser Oric was apparent for another obvious reason. Fire for food was a policy. Oric, if not a reluctant initiator, he became an avid advocate of this policy. The Prosecution's evidence will show that in addition to having been present at some of the attacks and seeing the actual destruction, Oric had firsthand knowledge of the damage. Also, Bosnian Muslims spoke to Oric about the burning and the escalating destruction of the surrounding Serb villages along with the plunder that inflated and devolved into black-market resources.
