utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No problem at all, Your Honour. As I stated, the Prosecution's evidence will show that Oric had firsthand knowledge of all the damages I spoke of. Also, Bosnian Muslims spoke to Oric about the burning and escalating destruction of the surrounding Serb villages along with the plunder and black market as a consequence. In addition, Oric had acquired notice or received information that could put him on guard that crimes such as looting, burning, and the mistreatment of detainees would occur. The accused saw the bloodied bodies and faces of detainees. He knew that prisoners had died under the watch of his guards. Oric knew that the leadership of the 2nd Corps command had warned that unlawful conduct violated the army regulations from May 1992 onwards. The Prosecution's evidence will show that he failed to prevent or stop the crimes and that he failed to punish or discipline his subordinates in the TO for those crimes of destruction and plunder. He failed to prevent the crimes, starting with the attack in Rakovici in June. He failed to punish since the Rakovici attack in June and he continually failed throughout the summer, fall of 1992, and the winter of 1992/early 1993. Naser Oric failed when he commanded the Srebrenica TO and failed when he commanded subordinates in the Srebrenica armed forces, and failed when he commanded the subregional group. He failed to prevent and to punish. The accused failed to punish the subordinates who destroyed and burned and looted. Why? Oric as a commander had been ordered by Lieutenant Colonel Knez not to burn or loot. Oric failed to punish because he did not disobey him by burning and by looting. On the contrary, his subordinates carried out his war plans and policies. Naser Oric maintained effective control over his subordinates. He issued orders and they were followed. He promoted, rewarded, and disciplined subordinates. He was feared by soldiers and civilians because of the effective control that he maintained. A commander is required to take the reasonable measures to prevent and to punish. To have effective control is, in essence, to have the ability to exercise and use reasonable measures available to prevent and punish. Oric could have issued orders and pushed forward decrees to prevent civilians and subordinates from burning and committing plunder. He could have ordered the prison guards to stop the abuse of the Serb prisoners, but he didn't. Naser Oric failed to create reasonable measures such as military courts or disciplinary panels in Srebrenica in 1992. He refused to use his police powers to arrest and to investigate and to charge his subordinates with war crimes or charge the civilians who accompanied those subordinates. Oric did not use the military judicial mechanism available to him in Tuzla. Oric did not report the crimes to his superiors, such as Colonel Knez or General Halilovic. Oric did not use the reasonable means available to him in 1992, 1993, 1994, or 1995, the means to punish the crimes charged in the indictment. The murder, destruction, and plunder took place within the context of an armed conflict governed by Article 3 of the Statute. Each of these war crimes - murder, destruction, and plunder - are proscribed irrespective of the nature of the war or the armed conflict. Starting with the first appeals decision of this Tribunal and until the most recent Trial Chamber decision, Judges have questioned the logic of sparing only victims of international crimes while being blinded at the pain of victims of internal armed conflicts. This has puzzled and troubled this judiciary. In this Tribunal, the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber examined evidence of wanton destruction and plunder. They had to determine if such crimes could only be recognised in an international armed conflict, much like Your Honours' task. They rejected the proposition of the Defence in that case and answered in the affirmative. Wanton destruction and plunder, two crimes governed by Article 3 of the Statute, happen and can be prosecuted in international armed conflict as well as internal armed conflict. That is also the Prosecution's position. The Prosecution will present expert and eyewitness testimony of the armed conflict. Evidence will prove that Bosnia Herzegovina as an independent country engaged in protracted armed conflict with the Republika Srpska and that Serbia encroached on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in April and May 1992 intermittently thereafter while the fighting with the Bosnian Serb army continued. Bosnia officially declared war on 20th June, 1992. The TO, the Srebrenica armed forces, and the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were engaged in armed conflict in the municipality of Srebrenica as well as neighbouring municipalities of Vlasenica, Bratunac, Skelani, Zvornik during 1992, 1993, and until the end of hostilities and the drawing up of the Dayton Accords. Prosecution witnesses who participated in the armed conflict as members of the ABiH will also confirm the existence of an armed conflict on the territory of Bosnia in the municipality of Srebrenica and surrounding areas. The attacking, plunder, and burning of the villages and towns not only had a nexus to the armed conflict, the Prosecution's evidence will conclusively show that these crimes were generated by Naser Oric's war plans and policies. Prisoners that met their death in the Srebrenica detention cell were first captured after the armed attacks on their villages. The prisoners who were killed, as well as the men, women, and children who survived detention, suffered imprisonment because of their capture during the war. Each was captured, guarded, and eventually released by enemy soldiers. The Prosecution's evidence securely establishes the nexus of the crimes to the armed conflict. The Prosecution would like to briefly address the subject of exhibits and documentary proof. During our case in-chief, the Trial Chamber will be asked to examine exhibits that are the paperwork of war, such as military orders, military reports, rules and regulations of military courts and disciplinary boards, as well as letters, telegrams, interrogation notes, soldier diaries, and medical certificates. The Trial Chamber will have to consider the ultimate weight of such documents. The Prosecution asks that Your Honours accept and consider the documentary evidence but that Your Honours, as the trier of facts, not be distracted by the camouflage net that Naser Oric will try to cast over the documents. The Prosecution will dutifully produce reliable, relevant, and probative documents that come before Your Honours through a chain of custody. One document is an order that originates from Lieutenant Colonel Knez, commander of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH. The order is dated 28th of May, 1992, and was specifically used to inform unit commanders of the TO of proper military conduct. It ordered commanders to, and I quote: "First, prevent burning and looting of movable property of the population during and after combat actions; second, prohibit all forms of physical abuse and massacre of the population; third, treat enemy soldiers and commanders who are taken prisoner or wounded humanely and correctly, in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions and the rules of the international laws of war." The Prosecution will prove that Naser Oric was the commander of the Srebrenica TO on the 28th of May, 1992, and thus directly subjected to the command and the orders issued by Lieutenant Colonel Knez. An order dated 20th of May, 1992, signed by Naser Oric as the commander of the Srebrenica TO shows that Oric appointed soldiers to the Srebrenica Territorial Defence. The Prosecution handwriting expert examined this order and confirmed that it is highly probable that Naser Oric signed this order. The Prosecution con --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry to have to get to my feet but we're entering into an extraordinary level of detail in an opening speech, and my concern is if we will have time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will certainly have the 90 minutes that you required, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And even more if that is required in the wake of some of the issues that are being brought up during the opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is important, so I will give you all the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm a little bit confused. Let me start again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I know where I am, but to make my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were just saying that you had this document examined by a calligraphic expert and that he confirmed to you that it is highly probable - that's the words you used - that it was signed by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I consider this as an introduction, Your Honour. Thank you very much. So the Prosecution contends that Naser Oric was a commander by the 28th of May, 1992, and as such was subject to the direct orders of Lieutenant Colonel Knez not to loot, burn, or kill and to treat prisoners humanely according to the Geneva Convention and the international laws of war. Other documents and exhibits, such as telephone intercepts of Naser Oric's conversations with Sefer Halilovic, or video footage of the accused, will assist the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution will offer documents and exhibits to highlight the criminal conduct of Naser Oric. I will address the issue of the witnesses. The Prosecution will call both Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Muslims to testify. The Bosnian Serb witnesses are the survivors of the military attacks in Ratkovici, Jezestica, Fakovici, Bjelovac, Sikirici, Kravica, and Siljkovici. Many of these Bosnian Serbs witnesses are rural country dwellers from small villages. They were inhabitants of Srebrenica municipality or nearby Bratunac municipality. The evidence will show that they lost their homes, were deprived of their livelihoods, and many lost their loved ones forever after the Muslim attacks on their villages. Killings of family members, neighbours, and friends will form part of the circumstances of the attacks prior to the crimes as charged as plunder and destruction of property. This is not a trial about those killings during the attacks. The Prosecution has not charged the accused with these killings. The Trial Chamber will deliberate upon the testimony of Bosnian Serb witnesses who recount their detention in the municipal building. Men and women will testify about the horrific mistreatment inflicted on the men and the control that Naser Oric had over each detainee until exchanged. The Prosecution will also call Bosnian Muslim witnesses to testify. Many of these witnesses were soldiers in 1992 who fought in combat operations for the survival of the Bosnian Muslims of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Vlasenica. Others worked in federal or local government of Bosnia and Herzegovina as civil servants, politicians, judges, police officers, or medical personnel. The Prosecution witnesses will carefully give their evidence before this Trial Chamber. After having risked their lives in the war for their Muslim loyalties, they now come forward with the attendant risk of being characterised as disloyal or even worse. These witnesses will testify about the acts and also the character and conduct of Naser Oric. Many of these witnesses, as colleagues or compatriots, urged Naser Oric to use more professional officers. Oric should have compensated for questionable experience. Instead, he acted with increased traits of arrogance, recklessness, imprudence, ignorance. The witnesses will narrate that Muslim soldiers asked Naser Oric to set up military courts and prisons in Srebrenica and to confront the lawless acts of Muslim soldiers. Oric refused and thereby permitted the disorder to mount. Witnesses will talk about how some of Oric's military missions were ill-conceived and irresponsible. Their evidence will show that Muslim military staff loyal and proud to have been led by Naser Oric felt forced to resign from the military staff post because of the increasing lawlessness in Srebrenica and because Naser Oric did not diligently exercise responsible command in time of war. In a revealing letter of resignation, the headquarters staff said, and I quote: "We will not accept the guilt or burden our consciences that the liberation of new areas from occupation only increases crime and destruction of private and socially owned property. Many institutions are not doing their part of the work. This is dangerous at any time, but particularly so now." Other Muslim witnesses will testify that they and others favoured the relocation of the Muslim refugee population to safer territory where food and shelter were available. It will also become obvious to Your Honours that there was military support for the removal of civilians from Srebrenica. Nurif Rizvanovic and his unit of 450 soldiers offered to evacuate the Muslim civilian population because it was difficult to protect them in Srebrenica. This support was rejected by Naser Oric. Oric's refusal of aid by his fellow Muslims was not due to his age and military or political inexperience but because Oric sensed that the reasoned and realistic proposals would present a challenge to his power. Unchallengeable, unsharing, unrivalled, in Srebrenica only one person had supreme power. No one should challenge him on anything. He kept no counsel. Quite simply, Naser Oric was apparently drunk with power at his age. Naser Oric did not countenance challenges to his military power nor political power. Naser Oric was in control, indeed effective control of his troops. He presided over local politicians. He was in constant communication with his troops and with local politicians and civilians. He was in selective, often sporadic communication with his superiors, often because of his own choosing. Little, virtually nothing, occurred in the town of Srebrenica or the municipality of Srebrenica without Naser Oric's knowledge or his approval. When a soldier or civil servant or politician's conduct ran counter to Naser Oric's wishes, he acted, he punished, he reprimanded, he ousted them. Consolidation of power propelled Naser Oric. The Prosecution's evidence will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Naser Oric is liable for the crimes of his subordinates who committed acts of wanton destruction of villages. Naser Oric is liable for the crimes committed by the civilians and soldiers. He instigated and facilitated the plunder of private and public property of Serb villagers. The Prosecution's evidence will prove that Naser Oric is guilty of the murder of the prisoners and the cruel treatment of the prisoners. The 1992 and 1993 the fight for Srebrenica was fought between the Bosnian Serb army and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Examination of the war crimes that had happened in 1992 and 1993 in Srebrenica is the first focus of this case. Other Trial Chambers have deliberated upon and condemned the international crimes, including the deportation and genocide of Bosnian Muslims that happened in the 1995 year. Your Honours' responsibility while contemplating the evidence in this trial is different. It is the conduct of the actors at the beginning of the Srebrenica war story that demands our undivided attention. When we train our eyes beyond March 1993, it's only to ascertain whether Naser Oric continued the impunity of failure to prevent or punish his subordinates for the burning, looting, and deaths of prisoners committed against Bosnian Serbs in 1992 and 1993. The Prosecution's evidence demonstrates that Naser Oric's position as a military commander went from a position of ever-increasing strength and control from 1992 TO commander to 1995 brigadier general, and that he commanded more than 10.000 troops, a formidable responsibility that cannot hide between an excuse of youth. In each succeeding year, he failed to punish those liable. Instead, he rewarded those soldiers and he accepted awards for himself. Soon after the Office of the Prosecutor conducted an interview with Naser Oric, he gathered his former fighters together in a meeting. He told them that the Office of the Prosecutor might also interview them about the crimes committed in Srebrenica between June 1992 and March 1993. At that meeting, Naser Oric issued a last instruction in regard to the Office of the Prosecutor's investigation. He told them, if asked, "blame it on the dead person." Naser Oric planned to blame his crimes on the dead Muslim fighters. I come to the finalisation of my statement, Your Honour. The Prosecution takes the time now at the start of trial to extend its appreciation to the Trial Chamber for earnestly listening to these opening remarks. The Prosecution is certain that the Trial Chamber will undertake its solemn responsibility to carefully contemplate and weigh the evidence presented at trial. Let me end my statement with a closing reflection. The warrior follows a code, one that places his actions and duties within the laws of armed conflict at all times, even more so and especially when chaos abounds. The warrior as commander understands and respects the purpose and limits of military attacks, the limits of military necessity, and the customary prohibition against destruction and plunder of homes and the ruining of lives. The warrior as commander understands and respects his established duty to provide humane treatment for all who are captured and detained by his fighting force. Only the warlord as commander could inflict inhumane treatment to prisoners. Cruelty and death as a result of such cruelty breaks the laws and customs of war and blemishes the noble code of the warrior. Only the warlord as commander would manipulate the law to his own will and deform such law from a noble code into personal manifesto. The warlord shields his crimes behind a false pretense of military necessity or claims of helplessness in the face of emergency and chaos. The truth is that Naser Oric, to preserve his military and political power and to promote himself, chose to obey the laws of war only when he deemed them convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Irrespective of the character of an armed conflict, only legal standards governs a commander's conduct at war. The warrior who descends into lawlessness and who promotes lawlessness is simply to be condemned. The evidence will show that the truth is that Naser Oric camouflaged his mantle of warlord under his uniform of a military commander. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, if this is agreeable to you, I was going to suggest that instead of you starting now and then we have a break and then you continue, we'll have the break now so that then you can start and finish your opening statement without any interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My only concern, Your Honour, is that I will certainly be 90 minutes long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. If we stop now and reconvene at 12 noon, then you have 90 plus another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a break and reconvene at approximately 12.00 noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicols, we are all ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones. We are all ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Obliged, Your Honour. May it please Your Honour, the Defence opening speech will be around 70 minutes interspersed with approximately 20 minutes of video footage divided into five clips, so an hour and a half in total, approximately. Your Honours, you are hearing from us now at the very outset of the trial, because in our view justice cannot be done in this case unless you have a true picture of what was happening in Srebrenica at the time of the events covered in this indictment, and you won't get it from what you've heard this morning from the Prosecution. So we are going to start the case by painting a picture of Srebrenica for you and we are going to do so with the use of four words. The first is genocide, a word which will always be associated with Srebrenica. The whole worlds knows of Srebrenica and the extermination of its Bosnian Muslim population by the Serbs in July 1995. The genocide started long before then. It began with Serb ethnic cleansing in early 1992 throughout Eastern Bosnia and continued right through the period covered by this indictment. International observers were warning of an impending genocide in Srebrenica, using that very term, as early as January 1993. Long before the final end game, the hangman had put the noose around Srebrenica's neck. It only remained for the condemned man to fall through the trap door. Srebrenica fell in July 1995 and what followed was Europe's worst massacre since the Second World War. 7.000 or more defenseless civilians were moved to the killing fields were they were murdered in the most cowardly and despicable way, blindfolded, shot in the backs, and buried anonymously in mass graves. Genocide. The second word we would ask Your Honours to have in mind throughout this trial is siege. Srebrenica, from 1992 onwards, was besieged, isolated, encircled, terrorised. Surrounded by minefields, Serb heavy artillery on the surrounding hills, Serb infantry in the towns and villages, Serb tanks and transporters on the roads, and Serb-run concentration camps like Susica or Karakaj on the periphery. Srebrenica was constantly surrounded by a cordon of death. Why was Srebrenica under siege at this time? Why was it and the other eastern enclaves, Gorazde and Zepa, an enclave at all? It was an enclave for the simple but chilling reason that the Serbs from April 1992 onwards had ethnically cleansed all the Bosnian Muslims from the surrounding areas. As Larry Hollingworth, the UNHCR chief, put it in March 1993, the Serb army: "Chased innocent women and children from village to village until finally they are cornered in Srebrenica, a place from which there is no escape and where their fate is to be transported like cattle or slaughtered like lambs." The Serbs carried out ethnic cleansing in order to annex the territory of Eastern Bosnia so that it could become part of a Greater Serbia, according to a well-executed plan. The enclaves stood in the way of a Greater Serbia, therefore they had to be eliminated. That is a matter of public record. Not into ethnic strife, the tribes of Yugoslavia running amuck, as the Prosecution has portrayed it, but planned, deliberate ethnic cleansing. Ethnic cleansing to create a Greater Serbia is the very basis of a large number of the indictments before this Tribunal; the Vlasenica indictment, Dragan Nikolic, the Foca indictment, the Deronjic indictment involving crimes against humanity committed by Serbs in Glogova, near Bratunac, an adjacent municipality and one covered in this indictment. The Karadzic, Mladic, Plavsic, Krajisnik, Milosevic indictments all deal with Serb ethnic cleansing. Srebrenica was a direct product of this violent ethnic cleansing campaign in Eastern Bosnia in early 1992 which brought refugees from surrounding towns such as Bratunac and Zvornik into Srebrenica. In that connection we would like to show you a short clip, 2 and a half minutes long, of a BBC programme relating to the ethnic cleansing in Zvornik in April 1992. If the video booth would please play video 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: THE NARRATOR: In a village 2 miles south of Zvornik we came upon the human calamity which is the practical result of all this. 2.000 Muslims are stranded and struggling to get out. They spoke of the fighting they had left behind them, the murder and hostage-taking which went with it. Different things are happening now. They have been happening since 2, 3 days. It's a terrible trail of terror which has been made and which is being made right now. You can hear even now some shells. We could and so could the refugees waiting for rescue. The artillery barrage was creeping towards us in the villages on the Muslim side of Zvornik. What is happening, she says, is that we are unarmed and they are firing at us. He begs the worlds to help them against the aggression of the Serbs and the federal army. The cry as we leave is again for help as quickly as possible, and the applause is only because we are the first sign they have had in days that anyone out there cares about their plight. Numbers are difficult to estimate, but in single file on mountain paths and in great columns on the wider tracks, it is possible that as many as 20.000 people are on the move, most of them by foot. These have been walking for two days, they have gone 18 miles and at least another 20 to go along this trail of tears. They were heading for the safety of a Muslim area without any help; no food, no medicine, and no transport, but all that they were talking about was the actions of the Serbs in their town of Zvornik. They killed all people. Something -- some peoples from the -- from the -- from the Serbian forces had something like a wire put on the neck and pulled. It is a great and tragic displacement of people, thousands of them being driven from their homes for no other reason than the Muslims are weaker and the Serbs are stronger and the ethnic map of Bosnia is being redrawn. The refugees are looking for help to the European Community, to the United Nations, and the Commissioner for Refugees. There's not a sign here of any of them. Martin Bell, BBC News, on the road from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And thus, Your Honours, in this very same area, the very time period covered by this indictment hundreds of Muslims were being killed in towns and villages in Eastern Bosnia such as Hranca, Glogova, Suha, Bljeceva, Borkovac, Mihajlovici, Krasan-polje, Bratunac, Podcaus, Voljevica, Zaluzje, Abdulici, Bjelovac, Zapolje, Tegare, Nova Kasaba, Joseva, Jagodnja, Vlasenica, and Zaklopaca. You'll see all these towns and villages during the course of the trial. They're dotted around Srebrenica. In every one of them Serbs liquidated and expelled Muslims in great numbers and herded them towards Srebrenica, an important fact which you may think the Prosecution might have mentioned in order to provide you with the full picture. Indeed, you might start to wonder as the Prosecution evidence unfolds whether you are being asked to believe in an Alice-in-Wonderland world where black is white and white is black, where the attackers claim to be the attacked and the besiegers claim to be the besieged. In this case will the Prosecution lead you into a hall of mirrors where you will be asked to believe the very opposite of what all the other cases of this Tribunal teach us about the Bosnian conflict? It will be a matter for you to judge. The facts, however, are inescapable. You will learn during this trial how Srebrenica, from the start of the war, was an open-air concentration camp, how tens of thousands of refugees were squeezed into the enclave, how they had to sleep out in the open in mid-winter because there was no room in the public buildings for all of them, how they were shelled and shot at by the Serbs like fish in a barrel, with people dying every day. The Serb army was vastly better equipped than the Bosnians, possessing heavy artillery, mortars, cannons, multiple rocket launchers, howitzers, tanks, and aircraft that they inherited from the JNA or received in support from Serbia. They decided rather than to take the town in a frontal assault, which they lacked the manpower to do, instead to lay siege to Srebrenica, to encircle it and then blast away at the civilians penned in there with heavy artillery, grenades, and shells falling every day and decimating innocent people. That is what happened, as you will see during this trial. The Serbs were never going to leave Srebrenica alone. It and the other eastern enclaves stood in the way of a Greater Serbia. The river Drina was to be abolished as a border separating Serbs, so the non-Serbs in that area had to go. The Serbs were not in a hurry; they had time on their hands to inflict a slow death on Srebrenica through shelling, sniping, starvation, and disease. And that was their clear genocidal intent from the start. The next piece of footage, 2 minutes long, from November 1992, shows General Milenko Zivanovic, the commander of the Drina Corps, which was the Serb army based just a few kilometres from Srebrenica, talking of how the coming winter will help them to defeat the encircled Turks, i.e., the Muslims living in Bosnia. He says how the Turks in Srebrenica are cut off from those in Cerska, Zepa, and Gorazde. Then his men sing of how they will slit their enemies' throats. Could the booth please play video 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There you see the soldiers who laid siege to Srebrenica as they truly were - not victims as they would now portray themselves - but willing executioners, particularly in 1995. And the agonies of the bitter winter in 1992/1993, took its toll as the sub-commander intended and as the clips you will see in a moment from March 1993 show. The word "siege" has an almost medieval, primitive ring to it, and justly so. For what are a besieged population to do? What they are forced to do? They are forced to fight for their very survival, especially to fight for food. Men, women, and children in a siege are stripped to their bare essentials, reduced to the lowest form, in which it is, in the words of Thomas Hobbes, a "war of every man against every man ... continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." That's how it was in Srebrenica in the very time covered by this indictment; a daily struggle to live in defiance of the enemy that would starve its inhabitants into submission. Which brings us to the third word: Starvation. Srebrenica in the period covered by this indictment was starving. For months the Serbs refused to allow UNHCR to bring in food and medicines. Why would they? They were using starvation as a tool of war against Srebrenica's Muslims as it was used, for example, in the Nigerian civil war. And some of the pictures you will see will put you in mind of Biafra. This is itself a crime under international humanitarian law. The Serbs, army and locals, had expelled the Muslims from their homes, farms, and fields, confiscated their lands and livestock, and chased them into the woods and hills around Srebrenica. There they found no food apart from berries, acorns, or bark on which they were forced to live like creatures of the forest. You will hear during this trial how civilians would try to get back to their homes at night to get food from their cellars, only to be killed in Serb ambushes or by Serb-laid mines. A great many people whose only crime was to have a terrible hunger in their bellies perished in this way. People famished, dying of malnutrition, slowly wasting away, would fight each other, maybe even kill each other, over loaves of bread or the aid that eventually came from the sky, like manna from heaven, in the form of U.S. air drops in March 1993. The footage you will now see of the people in Srebrenica with famine in their faces, wasted stomachs, and empty stares tells the story vividly, as do the UNHCR and other reports of the time. What follows will be the first of three extracts of news programmes broadcast by ABC News, with footage shot by Tony Birtley, a British reporter, showing Srebrenica in March 1993, the time of a massive Serb offensive in the time period covered by the detention charges against Oric. This first clip is seven and a half minutes long. If the booth could play video 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: THE NARRATOR: It just seems to keep getting worse out of Bosnia, numbing us with its relentlessness. We get shocked anew each time we see the pictures, and today for the first time we get a glimpse of life in Eastern Bosnia, an isolated, mountainous area where thousands of Muslim refugees are slowly starving as the United States searches for ways to get food to the people without getting involved in their war. When the Serbs refused to let United Nations relief trucks travel into the Muslim areas of Eastern Bosnia, the U.S. started dropping supplies from the sky. For weeks now the U.S. Air Force flying out of Rhein-Main Air Force base has carried tons of food and medicine to the people of Bosnia, while the American people wonder whether the supplies are getting through, whether they're doing any good and whether any of the factions have devised a way to use food as a weapon. We have seen the eerie pictures of American planes dropping their bulky beacons of survival. Tonight we see where the parcels land, and surprisingly, the first sign of an American military man on the ground in Eastern Bosnia. He's witnessed the impact of the air drops. These scenes come to us from the town of Srebrenica, a place almost impossible to get to. ABC's Tony Birtley finally managed it last week in what can only be described as an heroic effort to let us see what's happening in Srebrenica, Tony travelled by foot and by horseback to get into the isolated area. Since he arrived, he's run out of food and been injured by Serbian fire, but still he smuggled out the story. Nightfall in Srebrenica and people light fires on the streets and the hillsides to wait for what they call "the planes from God." After 11 months under Serbian siege, the U.S. air drops of humanitarian aid are their only lifeline. In the dead of night they make their way to the place where the prepared meals have landed, most often on steep-sided hills where people have to crawl up on their hands and knees. For some, like this lady, it's too much. She collapsed from exhaustion. But the shape of a U.S. parachute hanging in the trees, showing the drop spot. Gun fire echoes around as the army try to control the people and the supplies. I found this about 600 yards uphill. I don't know what it is, it could be medicine or something. The lucky ones clutch their treasure package of 12 meals and head home. But in the morning, the empty packets lying on the mountain track showing that some were so desperate for food they couldn't wait. American planes have successfully air dropped aid into this area for the last five nights running. The villagers say they received only one prepared lunch packet, the rest has been taken by the army. Most people have been eating only bread made from hay and corn for the last two months. That has finished. They now make it from the flour from a hazelnut tree. The father of this family demonstrates how much weight he has lost in the last 11 months. It is not a famine situation here but it can be best described as slow starvation. This is what I eat. This is what we eat. We've got nothing to eat. We're starving to death. We're practically naked and barefoot. Look at us. We're all in rags. We haven't had anything to eat. The air drops have worked but the people need land convoys which are continually being blocked by the Serbs. So far, we have been right on the money. I see MRE packets everywhere, I see people carrying MRE supplies, however we need to change our distribution now to flour, sugar, oil, and other basic necessities. These are very hungry people and they need basic supplies, not high calorie items like MRE. Right now we have done the bare minimum to keep them from starving and from dying, however we need to do a lot more. General Philippe Morillon, the commander of UN forces in Bosnia, visited the town. He told the authorities that he would open up road corridors to get food in and order the placement of military observers in the town that he hopes will deter shelling that locals say comes from across the nearby Drina river in Serbia. But the Serbs have so far failed to give their agreement to the general's plans. Just as General Morillon tried to leave, hundreds of refugees, many of them recent arrivals from Konjevic Polje, blocked his way. They chanted for peace and food and believed that if the UN commander left, the Serbs would start shelling. The tanks are about and waiting to attack. If you will leave, they will come and attack us. I heard the news that General Mladic will attack Srebrenica. We just want bread. We want the blue helmets to protect us. They kept their vigil all night around fires and in the end General Morillon decided to stay until a cease-fire takes effect and the Serbs allow UN helicopters to fly into Srebrenica. I've discovered, arriving here, that the situation was worse than I feared myself. And I understood the real fear, anguish, panic of this population. And I wonder too that their desire for me to stay here was probably the best solution in order to help them to survive here. The refugee problem is so acute that people have been forced to live in forests in homes made of logs. They're even worse off here, miles from the nearest road, with no hope of aid or medical treatment. These people say two elderly and three children have died here of starvation in the last few weeks. Refugees continue to flood into the town, most from Konjevic Polje where the fighting has intensified. Ten women and children were killed on Friday in Serb shelling, and 30 were wounded, including two UN soldiers. There were a lot of people there, a lot of people we saw last night on the streets, a lot of people who are sleeping in very, very cold schoolrooms. There are a lot of people who genuinely have had absolutely no food for three days. Children, women, old people, no food for three days, and there's no prospect of food at the moment. 150 alone are sleeping in this cramped room. They lie on the floor, on tables, and even under them. Srebrenica simply can't cope with this huge influx of refugees. Several hundred are arriving each day. They arrive tired and hungry, desperate not only for food but for shelter as well. This 75-year-old lady lays exhausted after a trek of 17 hours across mountain tracks. There is no food to feed her and she'll probably die within a few days. The sense of hopelessness here is increasing. For some, General Morillon's words were a kind of comfort but few believe they will change the fortunes of this battered people. Tony Birtley, ABC News; Srebrenica, Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, seeing those clips, one is reminded of the words of Primo Levi, who wrote in The Truce of his release from concentration camp: "Only after many months did I lose the habit of walking with my glance fixed to the ground, as if searching for something to eat or to pocket hastily or to sell for bread." How long, one wonders, did it take the inhabitants of Srebrenica, those who survived, to lose that very same habit? Srebrenica at this time was also without a water supply, electricity, telephones, and essential medicines; all cut off by the Serbs. Doctors in the war hospital had to amputate gangrenous limbs without anesthetics in conditions reminiscent of the Crimean war. Bandages had to be used and re-used without detergent or disinfectant. Skin diseases, lice, gastroenteritis ravaged much of the population. And thus people died of minor wounds and diseases which would have been preventable if only the Serbs had let medicines in. And thus disease too reigned, and that's the fourth and final word we want Your Honours to bear in mind throughout this trial: Disease. Srebrenica in this period was a living hell. The people were stalked by their very own four horsemen of the apocalypse; disease, starvation, siege, and genocide. Why do we mention all this? Well, we don't say that because the Serbs did this to innocent men, women, and children that the Bosnians could do likewise. We never have and never will seek to raise tu quoque as a defence. No. We raise these matters for their obvious relevance to a number of issues in this trial, as will become apparent during the proceedings, and also for this reason: International humanitarian law, the law applied by this Tribunal, was created to make war more humane, to tame the savagery of man and make gentle the life of this world. And so law which failed to take into account a humanitarian catastrophe of the proportions that befell Srebrenica, a rule of conduct that failed to give any consideration to the plight of a besieged, terrorised, and starving population would not only be a poor law, it would be inhumane and thus contrary to the purposes for which that body of law was established and contrary to the purposes for which this Tribunal was created, and contrary to common sense. For is it a crime for civilians to steal food from the enemy that is starving them into submission? Are they to be condemned for going back to the villages and fields from which they were expelled to try to grab some meager provisions that they had left behind? Should they have instead stayed at home, or more accurately, on the streets of Srebrenica where most of the refugees had to camp out and slowly wasted away and let their children starve, although every parental instinct would tell them to go out and search for food? Is that what people, parents, do? Is that what people are expected to do? Is that what the law requires them to do? Surely not. Is it plunder to steal weapons and ammunition from a vastly superior foe bent on your destruction, to capture those weapons in order to stop the Serbs from killing you and so that you can fight back? Especially, I might add, when your side is crippled by a UN arms embargo? Is it wrong to resist ethnic cleansing, to fight the ultranationalists who would expel you from your home simply because you are not a Serb and because they have a gun and you do not? Is it criminal to be unable to control thousands of desperate civilians from fighting for their very survival? It will be for Your Honours to decide. The Economist wrote recently, with regard to the conduct of the U.S. Army in Iraq, the largest and best-equipped army in the world: "Not everything goes right during war or military occupation, to put it mildly. Intelligence is always uncertain and often looks comically or outrageously wrong in retrospect. Decisions have to be made in a fog, on a balance of risks, in an atmosphere of doubt." You will have to imagine how much more true that is in a besieged town suffering a humanitarian disaster without proper communications and with thousands of refugees facing the daily prospect of massacre. You will have to imagine decision-making and trying to control people in that situation. Because the central issue in this case is whether the people in Srebrenica were controllable. To illustrate that setting, we would like to show the next clip, which is three minutes long, of footage shot by Tony Birtley in Srebrenica in 1993. If the booth would please play video 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: THE NARRATOR: To set the stage for us, what is it we're going to see and hear next? I think we're going to see one of the scenes that will stay with me, and I think for the people who saw the video, for many, many, many years, and that is the sight of complete and utter desperation of people who simply want to get out of a situation and are prepared to do anything to do that. I couldn't believe what I was seeing. I think sometimes in journalism we can be wont to steer towards hyperbole but there's nothing you could say to really describe what was going on; the sheer panic and the desperation of the people. And to see women to throw their babies into the back of trucks and hope that someone will grab them and take them to safety because separation, for them, was far better than having the youngster endure starvation and shells and bullets was terrible to witness. People getting angry before the convoy left. The UN heard about it but they could do nothing. I think people become so desperate they are prepared to do absolutely anything. I think it's the -- on the lowest level of humanity. I think these people are prepared to steal, even kill, to survive because nobody else is looking after them. I think in Eastern Bosnia in order to be a Bosnian soldier you've got to be resigned to be -- you've got to be resigned to injury, and also you've go to be resigned to death. It's a total mismatch. If it was a big fight, it would be the equivalent of Mike Tyson fighting some 15-year-old with both arms tied behind his back. They simply do not have weapons to compete on a level footing with what the Serbs have got. They have 1948, 1950 rifles; they have Kalashnikovs, if they're lucky. They've got a couple of tanks that they captured from the Serbs, but they can't fire them because they ran out of ammunition a long, long time ago. In my latter days in Srebrenica I went to the funeral of a soldier -- they're very common in Srebrenica because soldiers are being killed all the time. It was significant because he had been killed when there was a so-called cease-fire, everybody said there was a cease-fire, and suddenly we had the funeral of this 22-year-old young man whose head had been blown off, basically. There's a pitiful scene of his brother sobbing uncontrollably, distraught with grief, the father trying to hang to his emotions, to have some kind of semblance of dignity, and he sat there for a few seconds and held the hand of his son, his eyes welling up with tears.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, time and again during this trial you will have to put yourselves in the shoes of Naser Oric and to ask yourselves what realistically he could have done in this nightmarish world, this veil of tears that was Srebrenica from the outbreak of ethnic cleansing in April 1992 to the final genocide in 1995, because the law cannot require people to do the impossible. Yes, as the Prosecution has said, the laws of war were designed for war, but not all wars are the same. Not all involve genocide, siege, disease, and starvation. We make these remarks with regard to the crimes against property charged against the accused. You will remember that Oric is only charged on this indictment with crimes against property, plunder, and wanton destruction in the actions on Serb-occupied territory. Stealing - and I'm reading from paragraph 35 of the amended indictment - "cattle, furniture, and television sets." "Cattle, furniture, and television sets." You may wonder, and the public may wonder, why in this Tribunal set up to deal with terrible crimes such as genocide and crimes against humanity the Prosecution has decided to charge Naser Oric with the theft of television sets as a war crime. But they have and it will be for Your Honours to decide upon Oric's guilt or innocence of that charge at a time when people in Srebrenica were starving and being killed daily by shells. Naser Oric is not, however, charged with any violent crimes against people in these actions. The Prosecution seems to think so. They've referred this morning to how many villagers were killed during the raids. Well, they should read their own indictment. If there were a tittle of evidence against Naser Oric for crimes against people in these raids, you can be absolutely sure they would have charged him with it. He is not charged with touching a hair on the head of any Serb civilians in raids, nor of ordering, instigating, or aiding and abetting such crimes, nor even of failing to prevent or punish them. As regards crimes allegedly committed in the prison, in the town of Srebrenica, away from the front lines where Oric fought, again Oric is not charged with committing these crimes, nor of ordering, aiding and abetting, or of instigating them. Oric is charged only with having failed to prevent or punish those crimes. And he's certainly not charged with detaining women and children. Again, the Prosecution should read their own indictment. They don't charge it and if they had evidence, they would bring it. One wonders: Is the Prosecution's strategy to try to throw as much mud at Oric as possible in the hope that some of it will stick? This morning they've mentioned the black market, that Oric is a warlord, a former bodyguard, as if that has some relevance. Women and children, bloodied faces. Well, that's not in their indictment. As far as murders and beatings and the prisoner concerned, we say this: Nothing excuses such crimes, of course, if indeed they were committed in the way that the Prosecution say that they were. But the evidence will simply not bear out the charges that Oric is responsible for any such crimes. You heard what the Prosecution said this morning about the detention charges: Oric swaggering, prison guards, bloody faces, what was said by Oric to others. A lot of what has been said about these crimes we haven't seen in the statements disclosed to us and we don't know if we'll ever see it and we don't know if you'll ever see it. It's not true, it's not evidence, because the Prosecution comes before you today and says it. Just because the Prosecution leadenly repeats allegations, it doesn't make them true, obviously. So when these witnesses testify on the detention charges, I will ask Your Honours to take the transcript of Mr. Wubben's remarks today, have it in your hand, see every word what he said the evidence will show, and see whether the Prosecution evidence comes anywhere close to establishing those facts. It won't. So we would ask Your Honours to write down those four words that I mentioned at the outset - genocide, siege, starvation, disease - and to bear them in mind throughout this trial and to see as the Prosecution evidence unfolds over the coming days, weeks, and months whether it tallies with that reality. Your Honours, the Prosecution's approach to this case puts me in mind of a billboard poster that I saw many years ago in the United Kingdom which was an advertisement for the police force, and it was designed to test preconceptions. The first picture showed one man running down the street with a policeman sprinting behind him. The poster asks you what you think is happening. The misconception is that the man is being chased by the police officer, but in fact, no, a second picture is shown and you see that in fact they are both chasing a third person, a criminal, who is further down the street who is not shown in the first picture. Two men chasing a third man; that's the true picture. The Prosecution, it seems to us, wants to say to you: Just look over here in this narrow frame, this cropped picture, and just look at this act of plunder, this civilian leaving a Serb home with a television set, and judge Oric for that and ignore everything else that was happening all around; ignore the hell that was crashing around the ears of Srebrenica's inhabitants at the time. Just look where we want you to look, not over there at the things the Defence would have you see. Don't see the full picture is what they're saying to you. If you do that, you won't have the true picture and you would get the wrong answer -- I don't mean the wrong answer in terms of guilt or innocence. That will be a matter for detailed analysis of the evidence at trial. We say that will lead you to an acquittal at the end of this trial in any event. But if you follow the Prosecution's approach, you will not have the information necessary for you to weigh the facts properly and to apply the law to the situation on the ground in a judicious, comprehensive way. Many Prosecution witnesses may also try to avoid giving you the larger picture. Will they, out of a misguided sense of nationalism, or blinded by the propaganda that they have seen for so many years in Belgrade's media, try to bury the agony of Srebrenica's agonies? Will they deny that Serbs committed any crimes and that Srebrenica's Muslims suffered so terribly at their hands? In all probability many of them will, and you will have to consider what that says about their credibility generally. Remember that many Bosnian Serbs still deny the 1995 genocide and would have the victims be forgotten. The victims of Srebrenica should not be forgotten. We will now show the final piece of footage from Srebrenica in early 1993, the very period covered by the detention charges at a time when the Serb army was launching one of the largest offensives of the war in Bosnia, because a picture is worth a thousand words and images of a murdered people tell more than a statistic. This last clip, lasting six and a half minutes, is from a special ABC programme after Tony Birtley was evacuated from Srebrenica in March 1993. It provides a synopsis of the situation there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: THE NARRATOR: The village near Srebrenica just to be totally engulfed by hundreds and hundreds of people. I thought I was standing in movie and I kept expecting somebody to say, "Okay, cut," and then all these people with these gaunt, haunted faces -- and they all got expressionless faces. It's like life was drained out of them. Life was ebbing away. There was very little caring by the so-called authorities for the new arrivals. Nobody cared for the refugees. They were left for days on the street. No one cared anything about them. They arrived, and we followed a family through and they had been walking for something like 17 hours, and the mother carrying the little boy who had been wounded by shrapnel in the hand. He had been wounded at the same time as his father. They came, they didn't know where they were going. They had no relatives or friends. Where does this man recommend they can sleep? Where does this man recommend they can go? I don't know where. This camp has 60.000 refugees and there's only room for 10.000. Have you seen how many people are sleeping on the streets? We helped them carry the sacks. It was a very, very small gesture, but this woman was toiling under two great sacks and I must admit I found one sack very difficult and she had two of them. And it struck me that I can't believe that these people, they're people, and they didn't want to know. The father was treated in hospital and it was very tragic to see the little boy on the couch and the father on the couch and they had both been wounded. But that one -- so that finished them out because they can't have space in the sought-after wards because you can only have room for so many. It was never intended to be a hospital, more a clinic. It's not a place where you can get the best possible treatment, and even a surgeon, who I got to know quite well, was very honest about that. You would come in there, you would have an operation very quickly, you then would come out. You would have your stomach sewn back, shrapnel taken out as quickly as possible. If you were quite ill, you would stay in one of the wards. What the video cannot convey is the stench of unwashed sheets, unwashed bodies, of wounds becoming infected. I mean, they would always come and get me. They wanted to show me everything that was going on. Me, I was a way of telling the world for the first time that everything they have said is true. So whatever happened in the town, they would say: Get them, get them. They called me in to casualties. All these little girls in the town, you know. Five or six little girls had been hit, and the little boy as well. I mean, there was two screaming although they had very small injuries. But then there would be the 10-year-old girl who was lying and she had what I've heard so many times in Srebrenica and Sarajevo as well, what they call the death look. Her eyes are going blank. They had been hit. They were out playing in the south end of town, and later on I went to the home and one of them heard that her 4-year-old sister had been killed. She was killed instantly. And the mother went distraught and weeping and wailing. And like, you know, normal scenes, I think, in Bosnia. This is a normality. That's the terrifying thing about it. The medevac by helicopter was something that there was great uncertainty, especially by the Bosnian authorities. They didn't believe for a moment the Serbs would allow helicopters in and out of here, despite the fact that General Morillon was very, very confident. Well, after the helicopters took off with their first batch of wounded, within I don't know, two minutes, it was shelled. And it was artillery shells because you could hear that one coming in, huge bang. Roger. I have more incoming, more incoming. Over. The majority of the shrapnel sprayed to the south and that's why the two Canadian soldiers were wounded, because they were further south. When this huge, confused scene was going on in the hospital of patching up the Canadian soldiers, lying quietly on a bench was this 5-year-old little boy who had been badly injured in the southern part of town in a separate incident by a Serbian mortar. It was hoped that he would be evacuated with the Canadian soldiers. We went back down to the soccer field and the soccer field was shelled again. So the French colonel who had come in with the helicopters decided that there would be a medevac but no landing on the soccer field, so they had to be winched up. But before the Canadian soldiers had been winched up, the baby had died in the arms of one of the Canadian soldiers. It seemed to me that it is a great injustice in some respects to these people, that although we will put on a helicopter flight when it's dangerous to evacuate UN soldiers, we are not prepared to do that for a 5-year-old boy. And it's a most tragic scene: A father taking the little boy wrapped up in his golden plastic covering to keep him warm sobbing uncontrollably and his sobs and weeping were drowned out by the blades of the helicopters when it winched up the Canadian soldiers and went off. It seemed to sum a lot about Srebrenica and Bosnia, that basically these people, you know, they come second.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, these people who always came second in the eyes of the international community were the very people Naser Oric was trying to defend against even greater agonies than those you've just witnessed, if that is possible to imagine. Their faces tell not only of suffering but of fear, fear of what was to come. They knew the fate that awaited them, because the same thing had happened up and down Bosnia in 1992. From Prijedor to Bijeljina, from Zvornik to Foca, the same pattern of SDS-organised, arming of Serbs, disarming of Muslims, and violent takeovers of the municipalities with non-Serbs being systematically killed, raped, dispossessed, and the survivors expelled. As you will hear during this trial, this was done with the support of the JNA, volunteers from Serbia, police units, and paramilitaries, such as Arkan's Tigers, Red Berets, and so-called Panthers; David versus Goliath. The Muslims didn't have a chance. The carnage was such that by the end of the summer 1992 -- the transcript seems to be following the videoclip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I'm sorry to interrupt you for a while. Registrar, could you check the problem, please. Mr. Jones, we have to wait for a couple of minutes until this is resolved. You needn't worry about the time because I'm also informed that there is no sitting in the afternoon in this courtroom. So if we need to go beyond our scheduled time, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's fine now. So I've been told we can proceed. So, Mr. Jones, it's all yours again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if I need to repeat anything. I'll start from here. From Prijedor to Bijeljina, from Zvornik to Foca, the same pattern of SDS-organised, arming of Serbs, disarming of Muslims, and violent takeovers of municipalities, with non-Serbs being systematically killed, raped, dispossessed, and the survivors expelled. As you will hear, this was done with the support of the JNA, volunteers from Serbia, police units and paramilitaries such as Arkan's Tigers, Red Berets, and Panthers. The carnage was such that by the end of summer 1992, at least 300.000 Muslims had been cleansed from Eastern Bosnia and up to 40.000 killed in this period alone. 40.000 killed in Eastern Bosnia alone. The inhabitants of Srebrenica knew all this. They knew it from their own experience of Serb ethnic cleansing when the Serbs took Srebrenica in April 1992, killing and burning old people in their homes. They knew it from the bodies that they fished out of the Drina which had floated down from Visegrad where the victims' throats were slit by Serb ultranationalists on Mehmed Pasha's ancient bridge before the bodies were thrown into the dark waters below. They knew it from the refugees, like those you saw in the Zvornik video, arriving daily in Srebrenica from surrounding villages with tales of shellings, rapes, and killings carried out by Serb forces. The Muslims in Eastern Bosnia knew the reality; they were well aware from the start of the war that if they fell into the Serbs' hands, then that was it. That day would be their last. What could they do? Larry Hollingworth, at the UNHCR, summarised the dilemma well, writing of his visit to Srebrenica in March 1993: "We were in Srebrenica. I was metres away from families like my own in size, maybe also in background. I wondered how I would cope, snuggling my children next to me, attempting to ward off the bitter cold. I know that I would have felt humiliated, impotent, so I came to the conclusion that I would have stayed and fought. I then realised that these people had been driven out not by an advancing army - that was not the Mladic way - but by shell fire. You cannot stay and fight shells. They land and kill and maim indiscriminately. You can run like a headless chicken, you can stay in the cellar like a mouse, or you can quietly and resignedly join the throng and leave. Perhaps that is what I would have done. I felt close to the refugees but not close enough really to understand. Even if I had sat on the pavement with them, it could not be the same. I could escape; they could not. For me, it was now, but for them it was now, tomorrow, and maybe forever." Naser Oric and other local commanders, self-organised groups, did stay and fight. Oric was a young man, barely 25 years old, and a policeman when the war broke out. Having only completed his obligatory military service, he knew nothing of being a commander. But faced with the terrible decision, the likes of which we here are fortunate enough never to have to take, to flee his home or to fight, he and others took the lead and stood up for their right to remain on their lands and to resist the book-burning, mosque-destroying Serbian ethnic cleansing that the civilised world condemns. Oric defied the Serbs, and the fact is the Serbs never forgave Oric for fighting back. His crime, in their eyes and perhaps in the eyes of some in the West too, was not to lay down his arms and to allow himself to be slaughtered like a lamb, instead he and his men fought back like lions. Outgunned and ill-equipped, they fought in the only way possible to them, in guerilla warfare and in hard hand-to-hand combat. Oric was an outstanding warrior, leading by courage and personal example, never asking his men to do anything which he himself would not do first. He willingly placed his life in mortal danger again and again. Every time he and his men went to the front lines, they didn't know if they would come back missing a limb from stepping on a land-mine or with their bodies riddled with shrapnel or bullets; or even worse, whether they would fall into the clutches of the Serbs from which there would be no return, in all likelihood, only an agonising death. They chose this life over the trail of tears of refugees fleeing the Serb onslaught that you saw in the Zvornik video. Very few of Srebrenica's fighters are alive today. Many were summarily executed by the Serbs after capture in 1995 and before. Indeed, it is nothing short of a miracle that Oric survived and is before you today. That was the war he fought because he had no choice. This Tribunal wasn't established to outlaw war, much less the sort of defensive war Oric fought to save his people from starvation and massacre, nor was this Tribunal created to punish Oric for being a good fighter, for being exceptionally brave. The Prosecution has put Naser Oric's character into question this very morning, saying he ignored laws of war, regarded law as an irritant, that he was arrogant, reckless, impotent, ignorant, drunk with power, which I have to say is rather insulting to a Muslim even to use that term. The Prosecution claims to see into Naser Oric's mind, but we don't pretend to fathom anyone's soul. But surely it's not the business of the Prosecution to slur Naser Oric's character but to prove their case. Many, many Bosnian Muslims would beg to differ from the description they have given of Oric's character. What does that say about them if the Prosecution is right? The worst calumny uttered this morning was when the Prosecution said that Naser Oric told his men to blame the crimes on the dead. The Prosecution has taken statements from witnesses where that was put to them and they expressly denied it. One witness, as a matter of hearsay, said that he heard something to that effect. The Prosecution has statements from persons who fought with Oric and said, no, he never said that. We raised that in our provisional release application and submitted evidence from a misinformation campaign. Now, what are the Prosecution doing putting before you that sort of information which they know is false, which they know they have evidence to contradict? What we know is: From the moment Oric resisted the Serbs, they pursued him as their quarry. They pursued him in war and they have pursued him since in peace through propaganda, especially after the slaughters of 1995. In their misguided view, crudely put, if Oric can be made out to be the villain of the piece, if he can be found guilty of any crime, then they are excused for the 1995 genocide. And in an equally misguided view, the UN is then left off the hook for not protecting its own safe area. Therein we find the motive for Serb and UN apologists alike to rewrite the history of Srebrenica, to absolve them both of their sins towards the enclave. Your Honours, we mention these political undercurrents as a cautionary note only. There are those who would use the trial of Naser Oric as a vehicle for a revisionist account of the war in Bosnia. According to this view, the Muslims in Srebrenica, which they would have personified by Oric, brought the 1995 genocide upon themselves by conducting raids into Serb territory, that they were the architects of their own annihilation. The UN Secretary-General spoke to this repugnant and discredited thesis in the official UN report on Srebrenica. In that report he said: "The Serbs repeatedly exaggerated the extent of the raids out of Srebrenica as a pretext for the prosecution of a central war aim, to create a geographically contiguous and ethnically pure territory along the Drina, while freeing up their troops to fight in other parts of the country. The extent to which this pretext was accepted at face value by international actors and observers reflected the prism of moral equivalency through which the conflict in Bosnia was viewed by too many for too long." "... the prism of moral equivalency through which the conflict in Bosnia was viewed by too many for too long." Moral equivalency is the creed according to which a sniper on a hillside and the mother whom he guns down as she returns home are equally guilty. The soldier, drunk on slivovitz who lobs shells into a crowded town centre is no more good or bad than those he maims below, as they are all merely warring factions. It appears that the Prosecution has swallowed that creed hook, line, and sinker with their references to inter-ethnic fighting, describing an inevitable spiral in which the tribes of the former Yugoslavia were all at each other's throats. Nothing about planning for war, arming and equipping militias, as if what happened in the former Yugoslavia was only a natural disaster like an earthquake or a tidal wave. We will hear soon enough about that from Dr. Gow, the Prosecution's own witness. As a UN article of faith, moral equivalency is now dead and buried, as the United Nations report on Srebrenica from which I just read confirms, although it appears still to stalk the corridors of this Tribunal from which the Prosecution said this morning. The amoral credo, the moral equivalence, must not cast its shadow over these proceedings. For the purpose of this trial is not to resurrect and vindicate the dead peacekeeping dogma that all sides are equally guilty. It is the trial of a person, Naser Oric, who is presumed innocent before this Tribunal and who is entitled to an acquittal unless and until the Prosecution are able to prove his guilt to you beyond a reasonable doubt. It is worth taking a solemn moment to consider that principle, as it is the central pillar of any civilised system of justice. Naser Oric, as he appears before you now, is cloaked in complete and utter innocence in the eyes of the law. He does not wear the mantle of a war criminal or warlord simply because the Prosecution has chosen to bring this case against him. In fact, precisely because the Prosecution brings such grave charges, the presumption of innocence applies with all the more rigour. Would it not be the ultimate injustice for a young man who fought to defend his people from an enemy who had no qualms about slaughtering of men, women, and children, to be himself convicted and sentenced by this Tribunal if there is the slightest doubt as to his guilt? If there is any such doubt, Naser Oric absolutely and categorically must be acquitted at the end of this trial, not only for his sake, for the sake of his name, his future, his family, his people, but also for the historical record and for the record on which this Tribunal, too, will be judged for all time. If I may illustrate the presumption of innocence in another way, and I say this also for the benefit of those following this trial, there may be members of the public watching today who may know little of criminal justice or indeed of this case who will be looking at Naser Oric in the dock and thinking: What's he done? Well, that's precisely what the presumption of innocence isn't. A better question would be: I wonder why the Prosecution is bringing this case? Indeed that question may well remain in Your Honours' minds after the close of the Prosecution's case, in which event it will of course stop the case there and then. It's the Prosecution that brings the case against Oric and it's for them to prove the charges beyond a reasonable doubt. That's not a matter of proving possible guilt or even probable guilt. No, it's a matter of proving guilt so that no other verdict is open to you on the evidence. Naser Oric has a fundamental human right to a fair trial. That means, among other things, the right to be judged in accordance with the evidence - solid, reliable evidence - brought by the Prosecution in adversarial proceedings so that the Defence can challenge every item of evidence on which the Prosecution rely. The Prosecution this morning warned Your Honours to be aware of a camouflage net which the Defence would throw on dubious documents. I won't rise to that challenge now. That's obviously a matter for trial. But even in the pre-trial stage Your Honours have seen death certificates of the wrong people, Prosecution witnesses saying the documents looked fishy and may have been forged. Transcripts where no tape exists. Is it a camouflage net for us to raise these matters? The Prosecution would have you accept any scrap of evidence. So, Your Honours, you will have to sift out the many false, forged, and generally questionable documents which you've already heard about and which you will continue to see exposed as such during this trial. Oric is not to be judged on such doubtful material, nor is he to be judged on the basis of rumours, speculation, innuendo, dubious inference or leaps of faith that the Prosecution invite you to make. Naser Oric asks for no more than for Your Honours to look at the cold hard facts and to separate fact from fiction, the myth from the man, and when this trial is over, to deliver a just verdict. And we know Your Honours will do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. That brings to an end what we had put on our agenda for today. I wish thank you, Mr. Wubben, and you, Mr. Jones, for your cooperation, particularly for sticking to the time limits that we had indicated in the beginning. There are no further matters to discuss today. Tomorrow morning we will reconvene at 9.00. We will proceed with the guidelines that I referred to earlier and then we will try to sort out all the pending matters that remained unresolved after or at the end of the pre-trial conference. I should like you to make sure that we are put in the position to determine most, if not all, of them tomorrow. The whole sitting tomorrow will be dedicated to what's needed to be done before we proceed any further. Then, please God, on Friday we will start with the first witness.
